capitals.name: Jicheng (棘城; the 294 capital 'nearby Chaoyang')
capitals.note: One seat, not two. Murong page: 'Hui founded a new capital nearby the modern-day city of Chaoyang, Liaoning in 294'. Former Yan page: Hui made 'Jicheng (棘城, in modern Jinzhou, Liaoning)' the tribe's capital; Mohuba page: the tribe lived 'north of Jicheng (棘城, in modern Jinzhou, Liaoning)'; Murong Huang page: 'the capital Jicheng (棘城, in modern Jinzhou, Liaoning)', and in 341 Huang 'moved his capital from Jicheng to a newly built city, Longcheng (龍城, in modern Zhaoyang, Liaoning)'. Reading by the researcher (confidence 2): the 294 capital is Jicheng, so the earlier two-capital entry (Chaoyang to 336, Jicheng in 337) drew a move that no page records. The two placements lie c. 75 km apart (Chaoyang 120.42 E 41.55 N; Jinzhou 121.10 E 41.12 N); the coordinates are modern Jinzhou's, the three pages that name Jicheng; both places lie inside the land drawn. Before 294 the pages name no seat.

certainty.note: A steppe-edge tribal chieftaincy: no page gives a boundary or an area; the Daling basin round Jicheng and Chaoyang stands for the tribal land, eastern Liaodong for the 319 annexation, and the 285 Buyeo core is a raid drawn as the buyeo dossier draws it.

sources.title: Murong
sources.note: Murong history before Former Yan: Liaoxi after Cao Wei, 238 Mohuba, 246 Muyan, 283 Shegui's death, 285 Hui and Buyeo, 294 new capital near Chaoyang.

sources.title: Murong Hui
sources.note: Hui 269-333; vassal of Jin in 289; Duke of Liaodong 321-333; Yuwen campaigns 320 and 325; death 4 June 333. A thin page.

sources.title: Buyeo (state)
sources.note: 285 invasion of Buyeo by Murong Hui, King Uiryeo's death, Jin help reviving Buyeo (no year), territory.

sources.title: Former Yan
sources.note: Murong background to 337, Prince of Yan on 23 November 337, Jicheng, northern Liaodong, Murong Ren defeated in 336. Also: Murong feuds with the Duan and Yuwen round Liaoxi, northern Liaodong after Sima Yi's campaign, Ren rebels in eastern Liaodong, Jin vassal claim.

sources.title: Murong Mohuba
sources.note: Mohuba fl. 238-244; migrated to Liaoxi Commandery 'not long after the Cao Wei dynasty was established'; lived north of Jicheng (in modern Jinzhou); no year for the break or the submission.

sources.title: Murong Huang
sources.note: Capital Jicheng in modern Jinzhou, moved to Longcheng (Zhaoyang) in 341; Ren's post at Pingguo (Yingkou); Ren defeated early 336; Prince of Yan November 337; Jin titles 339-341.

sources.title: Murong Ren
sources.note: Ren stationed in Liaodong 319, Pingguo from 321, rebellion after Hui's death in 333, Duke of Liaodong 334, defeated across the frozen Bohai Sea in 336.

sources.title: Cui Bi
sources.note: Cui Bi's autonomy over eastern Liaodong; 319 coalition with the Duan, Yuwen and Goguryeo defeated, flight to Goguryeo, Hui annexes eastern Liaodong.

notes: Written by g-ea (gap batch) on 2026-11-01 from four pages. The English page 'Murong Xianbei' does not exist (url_not_found); the clan page 'Murong' carries the pre-337 story and is cited as the Wikipedia title. The state is a tribal chieftaincy in Liaoxi: pages give no boundary, no area and no seat before 294. Gaps: (1) the year the Murong settled in Liaoxi and submitted to Cao Wei is not on the pages, so 235 (xianbei's dissolve year) is a bridge at confidence 1; (2) the Former Yan page says the Murong held northern Liaodong by 337 and moved into northern Liaodong after helping Sima Yi, with no year, so no Liaodong gain is recorded; the Gongsun Liaodong dossier hands Liaodong to cao-wei in 238, not to the Murong; (3) Murong Ren's revolt of 336 is undated at its start; (4) Shegui's war with Jin and retreat 'to the upper Liao River region' (266-283) and Hui's 286 attack on the Liao River farmland are undated or only period-dated and are not drawn; (5) Hui's 307 'Grand Chanyu of the Xianbei' and the 317-318 Jin offer of the Duke of Changli (accepted in 321 as Duke of Liaodong) are titles, not land, and the Jin vassalage is drawn as one span 289-337 although 307-321 may have been independent. The 285 gain and 286 loss mirror buyeo's ledger lines 2 and 3; the pages say 'invaded' and 'captured ten thousand prisoners', not that the Murong ruled the Songhua land, so buyeo's loss would be drawn better as an occupation hatch. xianbei's successor land for murong-xianbei (the 224 shape minus the Southern Xiongnu) is far larger than anything the pages give the Murong and should be reduced to Liaoxi. Wikidata id left null (not given by any page opened). Family china-division follows former-yan, later-yan, western-yan and southern-yan, the Murong states that follow. Repair of 2026-11-01 after the review (reviewer fail): (1) the Murong land is no longer the whole gazetteer Liaoxi, which duan-liaoxi also draws 307-338: it is the Daling basin round Jicheng (Jinzhou 80 km) and Chaoyang (100 km) less yuwen-xianbei's Chifeng 150 km disc, with eastern Liaodong added from 319; the Duan and Yuwen lie south-west (Lingzhi) and north-west (Chifeng). duan-liaoxi's {region: Liaoxi} still covers most of the Murong land and its owner should narrow it to the Lingzhi country. (2) Murong Ren's revolt is a war with a zone (eastern Liaodong, contest 333-336) and the 319 annexation of eastern Liaodong from Cui Bi is dated from the Cui Bi page; the earlier gap (2) above is closed for 319-337 but the undated move 'into northern Liaodong' after Sima Yi's campaign (Former Yan page) stays undrawn. (3) The two capital entries are one seat, Jicheng in modern Jinzhou, with the Chaoyang placement of the Murong page noted. Still undated on every page opened (Murong, Murong Hui, Murong Mohuba, Murong Huang, Buyeo, Former Yan): the Murong break from the Xianbei and the submission to Cao Wei (235 is a bridge), the Jin-backed revival of Buyeo (286 is buyeo's bridge) and Shegui's clash with Jin.
